builds.title: 8x8 labz
builds.summary: A pocket sketchbook for 8x8 pixel icons, synced to one shared catalog.
builds.body:
It started with watching artists at live sketch events, each with a pocket
sketchbook, catching an idea the moment it showed up. I wanted the same thing in
my own medium: a page that is an 8×8 grid and ink that is light. There was a
practical reason too — old-school 8×8 icons had been hand-typed into C arrays in
noodlez-v2 and vizpow, every copy quietly drifting from the others.

So: one catalog, three ways in. A web app holds every icon and is the source of
truth. A handheld syncs it, browses it, draws new ones by touch, and plays them
on a real 8×8 WS2812B matrix. Any other firmware pulls the whole catalog as a
single `icons.h`.

## The handheld

An ESP32-2432S028 — the "Cheap Yellow Display" — with a 2.8" 320×240 ILI9341
panel and a resistive XPT2046 touchscreen, running LVGL 9 on PlatformIO. The
matrix hangs off a bare GPIO with no level shifter, 5V from VIN. Two build
targets: `cyd` puts LED data on GPIO 27, and `cyd-tx` puts it on the TX pin for a
one-cable build, with serial logging switched off so the log does not reach the
LEDs.

Sixty-four WS2812Bs at full white would pull about 3.8 A, so brightness is capped
at 40/255 and FastLED is held to 450 mA. How the matrix sits in the case is a
per-device setting rather than a constant — one lookup folds rotation, flips and
serpentine wiring together.

## The format

A frame is 64 palette indices, 128 hex characters, row-major from the top left.
The palette is global, append-only and caps at 256 colors; index 0 is black and
doubles as off. Icon numbers are permanent and icons are archived rather than
deleted, so nothing downstream ever breaks. Colors carry a family, usually six
shades generated from one base color in OKLCH so the steps look even.

## Living in 320 KB

| Budget | What's in it |
|---|---|
| 320 KB RAM | no PSRAM at all |
| 4 MB flash | 2.5 MB app slot, 1.4 MB LittleFS |
| ~50 KB free | what a TLS handshake wants |

That last line is the one that shapes the firmware. Every screen except Home is
built on entry and freed on exit, and that is what stopped sync rebooting the
board mid-handshake. Icons, palette and pending edits live in the flash cache, so
the whole thing works with the WiFi off. Sync runs on its own task on core 0 and
pulls only what changed since its cursor, twelve icons a page.

Edits made on the device queue in an outbox and upload before the next pull. Each
draft carries a hash of the server it was drawn against, so an edit can never be
uploaded somewhere it does not belong. If someone changed the icon first the
server answers 409, and the device keeps its version as a copy instead of
throwing the drawing away.

media.caption: The mobile version

entries.body:
Called the desktop case done. This is the last version of it.

Extended the base of the hinge, so an open lid has something behind it to lean on instead of flopping back. It looks better with that mass there too. Then the detailing: a silver skull inlay on the lid and a silver strip running along the base.

entries.title: Clamshell together, and a README

media.caption: 44 icons cached, last synced 52 seconds ago

entries.body:
Got the clamshell together. A printed threaded rod runs through a two-part hinge with a knurled head on one end, and there are detents at the knuckle interface so tightening actually holds the angle. Plain chamfers top and bottom, because the curved edges never printed clean and I stopped pretending they would.

Backed out the touch changes I made for the second board. The first board didn't want them.

Then the README, origin story included: a pocket sketchbook where the page is 8×8 and the ink is light.

entries.title: Projective touch calibration, and LED rotation per device
entries.body:
Touch was the day. Moved to pressure-based reads, threw out the four-corner min and max map for a projective calibration, and made the handheld run calibration on first boot instead of shipping my bring-up constants to every board.

LED rotation became a per-device setting in NVS too, because every matrix ends up mounted a different way in a different case, and a constant only ever describes the one on my desk.

entries.title: Another round of case bodies
entries.body:
Printed another round of case bodies and lined them up against the last one. No electronics in any of them. These were only to see how the shells come off the plate and how the lid sits shut.

Printing a clamshell is mostly a hinge problem. Everything else is a box.

entries.title: A day of just using it
entries.body:
No commits. A day of just using it.

Thirty-nine icons synced, stepping through them with the transitions running and the sync age up in the title bar. The matrix is still living in its own frame on printed knurled thumb screws.

The firmware is doing what it should. The enclosure is the open question.

entries.title: Renamed to 8x8 labz, and color families

media.caption: First build

entries.body:
Renamed 8x8 Studio to 8x8 labz, and redid both front ends neobrutalist: cream paper, black ink, thick borders, hard offset shadows, Slackey headings, lowercase everywhere, and a matching boot title card on the handheld.

The palette got split into families of six OKLCH shades. Picking a colour on a 320×240 resistive panel is now a family dropdown and twelve swatches, instead of hunting a 256-colour grid with a fingernail.

Home is four big tiles with a live mirror of the LEDs.

entries.title: Phases 5 and 6 — matrix player, touch editor, edit uploads

media.caption: 32 icons over two pages

entries.body:
Phases 5 and 6, one sitting. The matrix got a player with nine transitions and sixteen ambient patterns ported from vizpow.

Then the screens went in around it: browse, detail, settings and touch calibration. The editor came last, with pencil, fill, picker, eraser, undo and animation frames.

Two bugs worth keeping:

- the LVGL draw buffer has to be aligned, or the screen comes up blank and noisy with no error anywhere
- screens must be freed on leave, because the sync task needs about fifty kilobytes free for its TLS handshake and a leftover screen is exactly what it doesn't have

entries.title: Icon format, web app, and first light on the CYD
entries.body:
Whole spine in a day, both ends of it.

The web side first: the icon format and its shared library, a C header export, and a Postgres-backed API under the catalog, editor and palette pages. Deployed onto DigitalOcean App Platform the same afternoon.

Then the firmware. Scaffold, CYD bring-up, WiFi setup, and a first sync landing real icons in a LittleFS cache.

The panel fought back for an hour. Colours only come out right as BGR with inversion on, and the ILI9341 has no reset pin, so it keeps whatever inversion state it had across a warm reset and has to be told again at every boot.

builds.title: Noodle 2K
builds.summary: A one-tray LED instrument: an ESP32-S3 console driving a wireless fleet of panels, a disco ball and a dial remote.
builds.body:
A modular LED light instrument that turned into a distributed system, then got
pulled back together onto one tray. It's had three names along the way.

## Noodle → NoodleLab → Noodle 2K

**Noodle** (March 2026) was a breadboard: one controller, a few LED grids and
filaments, and a rat's nest of jumpers. It worked, barely, and every new surface
meant more wires.

**NoodleLab** (April–July) rebuilt it on an Adafruit FeatherS3 with STEMMA-QT
parts. When an external 8×8 hit the GPIO wall, every LED surface became its own
ESP32-C3 satellite over ESP-NOW: an audio sat, a 1×30 bar, 8×8, 16×16 and 12×8
matrices, a motorized disco ball and a haptic dial remote. It scaled by adding
boards, not pins.

**Noodle 2K** (from August 29) came out of a strip-to-bare-MCU rebuild. The
filaments and the PCA9685 went for good, the 16×16 moved onto a console pin, the
icon and 12×8 sats were retired, and everything moved onto one tray behind silver
diffusers. It's LEDs only now.

## What's running now

The **console** is still the FeatherS3, now with a 2.4" ST7789 mounted landscape
for a 320×240 UI and a Chladni resonant-plate visualizer as the screensaver. It
drives a 12×4 matrix, a 4×8 FeatherWing and the 16×16 directly. It never joins
WiFi: it scans channels 1, 6 and 11 at boot and runs ESP-NOW on the quietest.

Over ESP-NOW:

- a **1×30 RGBW bar** arc
- an **audio sat** with an INMP441 mic, broadcasting bass, mid, treble and beat so
  the whole fleet reacts together
- the **disco ball**: stepper, spot LED and OLED, on its own supply
- the **dial**, a round 1.8" knob with touch and haptics that mirrors the
  console's state
- two **HUB75 panels** on MatrixPortal S3 boards, a 64×32 and a 128×64, fed the
  same packets side by side until one is retired

**22 effects**, including a trimmed port of WLED's 2D particle system and a
16-band GEQ, all render through **23 palettes**. The hub75 panels also run the
**Patternflow bank**: JavaScript patterns hand-ported to C++, plus my own Mondrian.

**Controls:** three NeoPixel encoders, a NeoSlider, capacitive touch pads that pick
the target (matrix, disco or Patternflow), a nav encoder, and two Qwiic buttons.
Green steps patterns; red rolls a random palette.

## Why it's built this way

The distributed architecture wasn't a flourish — it was running out of GPIO and
refusing to stop adding panels. Moving each surface to its own wireless board
means the system scales by adding *boards*, not pins.

entries.title: Six wall patterns + a list browser on the dial

media.caption: The list, and the view after a tap launches it

entries.body:
Pulled six more patterns off the Patternflow wall: Fractal Storm, Branched Flow, Hypno Circles, Tri March, Vector Field Flow and Pattern 0522. Hypno Circles only exists as JavaScript, so that one is a hand port.

The importer had been seeing 44 of the wall's 194 patterns. The site caps a page at 44 whatever you ask for, and the loop read a short page as the end.

The bank is at 51 slots and still growing, which a grid on a round screen can't hold. The dial got a BANK mode instead: the knob scrolls a list, a tap launches, and once something is playing the knob does nothing. That also killed the old bug where a fast spin skipped patterns. Flashed the dial, Console and hub75, and the panel still lights with 14 KB more static RAM.

> **Next:** the rotation playlist is a 64-bit mask, so 64 slots is the ceiling until the protocol changes.

entries.title: Twisted Tunnel: a Bauhaus zoom, rebuilt

media.caption: Tilt 0, 0.25 and 0.5, then Color at 0.2 and 0.8

entries.body:
Started from a canvas sketch of Bauhaus rectangles zooming inward and ported it to the Patternflow bank as Nested Frames, bank 44. Named it Twisted Tunnel for the Patternflow wall.

The sketch claimed to loop seamlessly and didn't. Every five seconds each ring took on its neighbour's colour and shape. Keying every ring on its own index fixed it.

Then it drifted a long way from the original:

- **Tilt:** a twist keyed on ring size, so the frames form a spiral that turns as it falls.
- **Colour:** the red, blue and yellow from the Mondrian pattern, with true black and white.
- **Randomness:** each ring gets its own spacing, lean, shape and slow drift.
- **Fills:** about one ring in five carries dots, a grid, stripes or a checker.

I dropped the yellow square the sketch kept fixed at the centre. It looked weird sitting still while everything else moved.

> **Trap:** one float for zoom depth loses most of each frame's step near its wrap at the lowest speed, and the zoom stutters. Split it into a whole part and a fraction.

entries.title: README catches up with Noodle 2K
entries.body:
The README still described NoodleLab: filaments, the ToF sensor, the icon and 12×8 sats, 16 effects, a hardcoded channel. All of that has been gone since the August rebuild, and CLAUDE.md was the only honest document in the repo.

Rewrote it around what's actually on the tray, with the three-name arc up front so the old photos and posts still make sense. Merged the Mondrian branch to main on the way past, and deleted four merged branches that had been sitting there since spring.

entries.title: Mondrian, take two

media.caption: One layout at five settings of the Color knob

entries.body:
Reworked the motion. The old version slid one section out and back like a tray, and sometimes nothing actually changed on screen. Now every line moves at once while part of the grid rebuilds and a colour block slides to a new cell.

That turned up a bug where remixing the whole canvas skipped moving the lines at all.

The Color knob is one smooth sweep now, built on the spacing between Mondrian's own red, blue and yellow, with his palette sitting in the middle of the range.

Flashed it to the rig and every colour was wrong. Took me a minute to notice the global palette tint was still switched on, quietly re-mapping a pattern that brings its own colours.

entries.title: A Mondrian pattern for the Patternflow bank

media.caption: Three compositions from one run

entries.body:
Wrote my first pattern from scratch for the Patternflow bank: a Mondrian grid that keeps rearranging itself.

It builds a layout by splitting the canvas in two, then splitting the pieces, which is roughly how the paintings are put together. Whatever it lands on is a valid composition rather than a scatter of rectangles.

Worked it out in JavaScript first, in a small browser harness, then hand-ported it to C++ for the hub75. The two versions match pixel for pixel, which is the only reason I trust the port.

entries.title: Landscape TFT + chrome refresh; the Patternflow bank

media.caption: Kaleidoscope on the 64×32 hub75 and the 16×16, the dial mirroring
Second hub75 board up, both panels running

entries.body:
Recomposed the whole UI for a landscape 320×240 mount, because the ribbon was blocking the view in portrait: one-row header, framed menus, Live Control and Chladni both re-laid out. Landscape puts text beside its neighbours instead of into dead space, so every variable-length name now goes through a fitter before it's drawn.

The Patternflow bank landed the same week: JS shader-style patterns hand-ported to C++, running on all three boards. The red Qwiic button got demoted from "previous pattern" to a palette dice, because I never once used it as a back button. The dial already has back.

entries.title: 21 effects, a palette system, and 'Noodle 2K'
entries.body:
A content wave, and a name.

The effect catalog went to 21 with a trimmed 2D particle engine and the WLED particle effects on top of it, plus a real 16-band GEQ analyzer. Then the palette system: one global palette every effect renders through, with host-parity tests proving palette 0 reproduces the old look exactly, and a picker on the dial.

Rebranded the rig Noodle 2K, with a new layered power-on intro to match. Also brought up a hub75 MatrixPortal satellite doing native 64×32, which is four times the pixels of anything else on the tray.

entries.title: Killed a FeatherS3 with 48 pixels
entries.body:
Killed a FeatherS3. The 12×4's 5 V and ground were on the Feather's own pins, and 48 WS2812s at full brightness ask about 2.9 A from a rail good for roughly one. It browned out under bright frames for a while, then died, and wouldn't enumerate again even in ROM bootloader mode.

The wing is physically stuck on the Feather's rail, so that one is capped in software instead. Everything else draws from the PSU.

> **Trap:** `FastLED.setMaxPowerInVoltsAndMilliamps()` will not save you here. It applies one global budget and has no idea two strips sit on different supplies, so it looks like protection and isn't.

entries.title: The big rebuild — bare MCU, Chladni, cyberpunk chrome
entries.body:
Stripped the rig to a bare MCU and brought it back subsystem by subsystem. Things that did not come back: the icon sat, and later the 8×12, with the 16×16 moving onto a console pin instead.

What changed on the way:

- **SparkFun inputs** onto their own I2C bus, because the CAP1203 was picking up EMI from the Adafruit bus and reporting touches nobody made
- **Screensaver** replaced with a live Chladni resonant-plate visualiser
- **UI** redone on an anti-aliased chrome kit, which finally killed the flicker

A rebuild is the only time you get to un-choose things. I took it.

entries.title: Portability pass + matrix sat moves to an S3
entries.body:
Portability pass. Every board's `platformio.ini` now pins the pioarduino platform by URL, so a build on a new machine produces the same firmware as the old one instead of whatever the toolchain drifted to.

The 12×8 matrix satellite moved to a dual-core ESP32-S3 SuperMini for the better radio, and the 16×16 got a baked Pac-Chase animation as its own source.

entries.title: Disco-ball satellite — and a nasty ground-noise lesson
entries.body:
Added a motorized disco ball as its own satellite: stepper, spot LED, OLED, and a dedicated live target on the console.

The first version ran the stepper off main power and made the ground filthy. Noise bled through the whole Noodle, and it read like a data problem until I looked at what I'd just plugged in. Its own supply fixed it.

> **Trap:** a motor and your logic on one ground rail. Classic, and I still walked into it.

entries.title: ESP-NOW only, plus a screen-capture path
entries.body:
Dropped WiFi association altogether. The Console brings the radio up for ESP-NOW and never joins an access point, which means no router, no DHCP lease, and nothing to go stale between sessions.

Started the screen-share path as well, browser to ingest to matrix, with a LittleFS clip store behind it, so I can push real captured pixels at the 16×16 instead of only generated effects.

entries.title: Dial remote, sprite overlays, playlists
entries.body:
The dial sat became the remote: a live preview canvas, Qwiic forward and back buttons for the pattern stack, and curated playlists.

Added a composite overlay source too, a 16×16 pattern with a centred 8×8 icon on top, palette index 0 transparent so the pattern shows through the sprite.

Cut the dead DDP path out entirely while I was in there.

entries.title: The fleet takes shape — bar, 8×8, 16×16 satellites
entries.body:
Built out the pixel satellites: a 1×30 bar, an 8×8 icon panel, a 16×16 matrix. Each one is its own board rendering locally, fed by a shared wire format (v5) that carries effect state rather than pixels.

That distinction matters. Sending state means a satellite keeps animating at its own frame rate even when a packet goes missing.

entries.title: Audio satellite — first ESP-NOW peer, beat detection
entries.body:
The first satellite: a separate board with a mic, running spectral-flux beat detection with a bass lean, broadcasting audio features over peered ESP-NOW.

Every effect on every board reads the same bass, mid, treble and beat, so the whole rig moves on the same downbeat instead of each surface guessing on its own.

entries.title: Three encoders, per-target ownership, Source Map
entries.body:
Three NeoPixel rotary encoders, each owning a slot on whatever target is live. Slots are assigned by I2C address, highest address takes slot 0, so the wiring order decides the layout and nothing has to be configured.

Added a Source Map for assigning a source per surface, and retired Pixelblaze in favour of the native engine. Running two effect engines was one more than the rig needed.

entries.title: Descriptor-table effect engine + the FeatherWing
entries.body:
Stood up the real effects engine: a descriptor table with 10 effects to start, so adding one is a function and a row rather than a new branch in the render loop.

A 4×8 NeoPixel FeatherWing went on mirroring the matrix, and the filaments got a TPS61169 driver with gamma correction so a dim setting actually looks dim.

entries.title: Ran out of pins — going distributed
entries.body:
Added an external 8×8 and ran out of pins. Between the TFT, two I2C buses, the local matrix, the wing and the filament lanes, the FeatherS3 had nothing usable left.

The fix could have been a bigger chip or an expander. Instead every LED surface becomes its own ESP-NOW satellite, with its own board and its own render loop, taking effect state over the air.

> **Lesson:** when you're out of pins, stop counting pins. The system scales by adding boards now, and I've never hit the wall again.

entries.title: Filaments breathing, fiber optics, live Pixelblaze
entries.body:
PCA9685 filaments breathing on a sine offset, a Pixelblaze websocket path for browsing and streaming patterns live, and the `patterns/` scaffolding underneath.

First evening the thing looked less like a prototype and more like an instrument.

entries.title: Dual-core FreeRTOS — network off the render path
entries.body:
Split the firmware into four FreeRTOS tasks across both cores, with the network moved to core 0 so the radio and the LED render stop fighting over the same core.

Every piece of hardware gets exactly one owner task. That rule has survived every rebuild since, and it's the reason a WiFi hiccup doesn't stutter an animation.

entries.title: Noodle 2.0 — core up and running in a day
entries.body:
Rebuilt onto a FeatherS3, and got further in one sitting than the breadboard managed in a week:

- display, encoder and buttons alive
- a sensor dashboard for distance, light and the onboard NeoPixel
- WLED control
- a direct 4×12 matrix running an 8×8 icon slideshow

Solderless modules on one cable is the whole reason. Nothing came loose all day.

entries.title: Noodle 1 — the breadboard prototype that didn't scale
entries.body:
First pass at the idea: one controller driving a row of LED grids and filaments, built on a breadboard with a rat's nest of jumpers behind it.

It worked, barely. Every new surface meant more wires and more flakiness, and I could see the ceiling from where I was standing. Tore it down and went looking for a sturdier way to prototype, which turned out to be Adafruit's STEMMA QT modules.

builds.title: kFun
builds.summary: Three handheld game consoles built from one codebase.
builds.body:
A family of handheld consoles built from one monorepo.

| Spec | tinyfun | bigfun | megafun |
|---|---|---|---|
| Board | LOLIN S3 Mini Pro | ESP32-S3 SuperMini | ESP32-S3 SuperMini |
| Screen | 128×128 GC9107 | 2.0" 320×240 ST7789 | 2.0" 320×240 ST7789 |
| Input | 3 buttons | d-pad + two triggers | XY joystick + click |
| Layout | portrait | landscape | landscape |

tinyfun and bigfun run the same six slots, each game adapting to the hardware it
lands on: lean and legible on three buttons, grown into sprites and particle
juice on six. Sometimes the slot holds a different game entirely. Invaders
becomes Galaga on the wide board, Breakout becomes Arkanoid.

Tetris · Breakout · Snake · Invaders/Galaga · SkyGrid · Backgammon

megafun runs its own set on a joystick-native framework, and shares exactly the
piece that has to stay in lockstep: the backgammon rules engine and the ESP-NOW
link, so all three can play each other.

## How it holds together

`common/` never names a GPIO or a screen size. Pins live only in each board's
`Config.h`, and shared code branches on two capability flags those boards
declare, `KF_LANDSCAPE` and `KF_DPAD`. megafun is the reason there are two: it's
landscape but joystick, which one flag couldn't express. Adding a board means
declaring its capabilities, not adding a device identity.

The engine is a non-blocking contract (`init` / `update(dt)` / `render`) at a
fixed 60 Hz, with every game placement-new'd into a single 12 KB arena that fails
to compile if it won't fit. Two rules earned the hard way: the framebuffer is
pinned to SRAM because PSRAM faults on per-pixel writes, and the quit chord is
un-swallowable, so a misbehaving game can never trap you inside it.

Favourites among the six: **SkyGrid**, an original software 3D renderer with no
z-buffer that pushes 128 triangles at 60 fps, and **Backgammon**, fully
rules-checked and unit-tested, playing 2-ply expectimax on bigfun with a doubling
cube, Crawford rule and NVS match save.

picturesOverTime.caption: bigfun next to the smaller tinyfun
the finished bigfun

entries.title: m5bigfun on CoreS3, and a chooser
entries.body:
Ported the console to m5bigfun: a CoreS3 sitting in a Faces Bottom3 with a Gamepad3, and two rows of five SK6812 to play with.

The LEDs got a job rather than a glow. Effects are ranked by tier, every game has a voice on the strips, and Backgammon uses them to show whose turn it is.

Since the device also holds the vizBot firmware, there's a top-level chooser in the factory partition now: one board, two firmwares, pick at boot.

entries.title: Third-batch board enrolled
entries.body:
Enrolled a third-batch tinyfun board as panel profile B.

Every batch of panels drifts a little in colour and gamma. Cutting a new profile beats re-fighting the same tuning on each board.

entries.title: Shake to restart, and a printable case
entries.body:
A QMI8658C shake HAL: physically shaking the console restarts the current game. bigfun has no IMU, so it gets a no-op stub and the games don't care which one they're on.

The engine resumes from NVS too, so a game picks up where you left it. And the enclosure is packaged as a sliceable 3MF project now, one print from a shell.

entries.title: megafun folds in, three boards
entries.body:
Folded megafun into the monorepo. All three boards share one core now, and the differences live in capability flags each board declares rather than in forks of the code.

Per-board panel profiles landed with it, plus an on-board tuner, and the original tinyfun board is enrolled as profile M1. The launcher auto-rotates its attract cards after idle. Rewrote the README for three boards with a pre-commit guardrail, because a README about three boards will rot in a week otherwise.

entries.title: megafun: a tilted screen and a joystick
entries.body:
megafun was a way to keep expanding on what I was doing. I'd seen a tilted plane used as the support for a screen, and I had a small joystick lying around, so the two went together.

I wanted a marbles game, and you can't do marbles without a joystick. It led to exploring a lot of other things on the same base:

- **Marbles:** the tilt maze that started it
- **Chladni:** a resonant-plate pattern generator
- **LED Studio:** a menu for driving the LED cap on top

entries.title: Backgammon VS PLAYER over ESP-NOW
entries.body:
Backgammon plays over an ESP-NOW link now. Built phase by phase: turn transport first, then game-over sync, then the doubling cube, mirroring the megafun implementation so the two stay at parity.

Then a per-device mirror and a resilience layer, so one dropped packet doesn't leave two boards disagreeing about where the checkers are.

entries.title: Galaga trains and SkyGrid forks
entries.body:
Deepened the wide-board games. Galaga got enemy trains and a difficulty ladder; SkyGrid got track forks and ship motion that reads like a ship rather than a sprite sliding.

Both got UI effects that use the space the wide board actually has, instead of a small-screen layout stretched.

entries.title: Galaga on bigfun, README rebranded kFun

media.caption: the finished bigfun

entries.body:
Galaga takes the Invaders slot on bigfun, with auto-fire. Same slot, same launcher, different game depending on which console you picked up.

Rebranded the README as kFun, tinyfun and bigfun under one name.

entries.title: PSRAM enabled, Backgammon Hard AI goes 2-ply expectimax
entries.body:
Turned on bigfun's 2 MB PSRAM.

Then reworked the Backgammon Hard AI into 2-ply expectimax, so it weighs the dice a roll deep instead of grabbing the nearest legal move. It beats me now, which I'm choosing to call a success.

entries.title: Particle effects across both boards, and real Backgammon match play
entries.body:
Juice day. Particles and shake across both consoles:

| Game | Effect |
|---|---|
| Invaders | kill and death pops |
| Tetris | line-clear debris |
| Backgammon | checker slide and capture pops |
| Snake | glide |
| Breakout | brick-break and life-loss shakes |

Real match play landed in bigfun Backgammon: 5-point match, doubling cube, difficulty setting, saved to NVS. The intro got the Slackey wordmark with a glow and particles behind it.

entries.title: Merged into the kFun monorepo, shared console on the SuperMini

media.caption: bigfun next to the smaller tinyfun

entries.body:
Restructured into the kFun monorepo, a shared `common/` with `tinyfun/` and `bigfun/` as thin board ports on top, and got the full app booting on the SuperMini.

Then art and effects for the wide board, which is where the two consoles start being different games:

- backgammon in landscape, with traditional triangle points
- Tetris centred, with side panels either side of the well
- Breakout rebuilt as Arkanoid
- a sprite pipeline off the Kenney CC0 art
- attract cards on the launcher, nebula backgrounds with post-FX, a themed game-over screen

entries.title: Backgammon replaces Asteroids, Canyon renamed to SkyGrid
entries.body:
Swapped Asteroids out for Backgammon, renamed Canyon to SkyGrid, and added a help screen that lists the buttons.

Backgammon took the rest of the day: redrew the board, made a checker's second move findable instead of hidden, added bear-off auto and bigger dice. Cut the Slackey case logo SVGs while I was at it, for a shell that doesn't exist yet.

entries.title: First TinyFun boot on the S3 Mini Pro
entries.body:
First working console: a five-game handheld on the LOLIN S3 Mini Pro, 128×128, three buttons.

Boot screen and a custom typeface up, and SkyGrid's ancestor running on the panel as CANYON, a 3D anti-gravity racer. Gave Asteroids a 3-shot spread and thinned out the opening wave, because a full field of rocks on a 128 px screen is not a first level, it's a wall.

entries.title: Mini Tetris: parts and a first case
entries.body:
Everything for a small handheld, laid out on the mat: a printed case, a LiPo, a USB-C charge board, a slide switch and the screen board. At the time I was calling it Mini Tetris.

Mini Tetris grew up to be tinyfun.

builds.title: vizSpot
builds.summary: A 64×64 LED matrix that shows what Spotify is playing, and dances to it.
builds.body:
A 64×64 LED matrix that shows what Spotify is playing, and dances to it. The
cover is the real one, fetched and decoded on the board at full bleed, artist
along the top edge, title and progress along the bottom in a 3×5 pixel face. No
app, no cloud service, nothing left running on a computer.

## What it does

- **Now Playing:** the cover at 64×64, crossfading on every track change
- **Visualizer:** 22 effects out of the NoodleLab catalog, driven by a 512-point FFT of the board's own mics. 16 log-spaced bands, spectral-flux beat detection, 23 palettes, a new one on every effect change
- **Ambient:** slow patterns when nothing is playing, reacting to room audio so it still moves when the music is coming from somewhere else. A cover you played earlier fades in with how long ago it was
- **Kaleidoscope:** mirror and rotational folds over any effect, with live blend, spin and slice
- **Control page:** all of it from a phone on the same WiFi, plus Spotify search and transport. The browser talks to Spotify directly, so the board pays nothing for it

Giving one away needs no computer. The panel shows a QR code and the new owner
connects their own Spotify from their phone. The sign-in travels encrypted, so
the relay never sees it.

## How it's built

Arduino on ESP-IDF, five FreeRTOS tasks, one owner per peripheral: render, audio
and the thumb wheel on core 1, WiFi and Spotify and the web server on core 0.
Internal RAM is the whole design constraint.

| Internal, 320 KB | PSRAM, 8 MB |
|---|---|
| panel DMA buffers | the 64×64 canvases |
| WiFi stack | album art and JPEG buffers |
| one TLS session | track history, API bodies |

There is room for exactly one TLS context, so the Spotify API, the token
endpoint and the art CDN take turns, and whoever wants it drops the other's
keep-alive first. Two separate bugs came out of forgetting that.

The effect catalog is a dated snapshot of the shared library from NoodleLab,
with the ESP-NOW wire format cut out.

Browning out on a laptop USB port
De La Soul, The Magic Number

entries.title: Phone pairing by QR — and the panel in a finished case

media.caption: De La Soul, The Magic Number

entries.body:
A board you hand to someone shouldn't need a computer. So the panel shows a QR code, alternating with a typable base32 card for anyone who would rather not scan:

1. The phone scans it and signs into Spotify on kpow.xyz
2. The credentials come back as an AES-256-GCM envelope the relay can't read
3. The board decrypts, applies, verifies against Spotify, and acks

The first real phone test died on that last step: `ack ok -> http -1`, with the phone sitting on "Board is connecting". The Spotify client was holding the only TLS context again. Now the ack frees the keep-alive before it posts and retries for about 15 seconds. Re-tested on the second board: Welcome back, then You're connected.

The case is finished too. Printed frame and stand, skulls cut into the side panel, and a choice of silver, white, grey or translucent diffusers.

entries.title: Search straight from the browser, per-card saves, and the docs
entries.body:
Put Spotify search on the control page, with the browser calling Spotify directly through a token endpoint so the board carries none of it.

Most of the work was in what Spotify does when you ask it to play something:

- a limit above 10 comes back 400, so the search asks for 10
- playback needs an explicit device id, and a stale one has to be retried
- a browser player accepts a queue and then refuses to play, so the picker prefers real Spotify apps and warns you when you've chosen one

The page got per-card Save buttons and speed sliders for the visualizer and ambient while I was in there. Then the docs, all four: README, user guide, hardware guide, web API reference.

entries.title: Memory cards in ambient, kaleidoscope, and a neo-brutalist control page
entries.body:
Ambient got a memory. It keeps 20 tracks with their covers, seeded from Spotify's recently-played at boot, and fades one back in with how long ago you played it. NTP for the clock, PSRAM for the API bodies.

The rest of the day:

- **Kaleidoscope:** a post-filter over any effect, NoodleLab's fold modes, live controls on the page
- **Puzzle:** 16 px tiles on the 64×64, proportional borders, faster eased slides
- **Snakes:** rendered at 32×32 and upscaled, so the bodies are 2 px and you can see them
- **Control page:** neo-brutalist restyle, collapsible cards, transport buttons

Then a stuck-on-song bug. After a token expired the display never moved on, because the refresh was going out while the API session was still open.

> **Lesson:** there is room for exactly one TLS context. The API, the token endpoint and the art CDN take turns, and whoever wants it drops the other's keep-alive first.

entries.title: Status screens, random palettes, and a wheel that stopped missing presses
entries.body:
The thumb wheel kept missing presses and the decoder was not the problem. `loop()` was starved under the visualizer and the FFT, so the poll just wasn't running often enough. Moved it to its own 10 ms key task with latched presses, a rock guard, and a veto so a push doesn't read as a rock.

Three smaller things around it:

- **Status screens:** boot splash, WiFi connecting, setup, unreachable, and the three Spotify states, all redrawn
- **Palettes:** a new random one on every effect change, held per side through the crossfade
- **Brightness:** default up to 100%, ambient uncapped

entries.title: First light: not the board the listing said, and USB can't feed it

media.caption: First light
Browning out on a laptop USB port

entries.body:
The board is not what the listing said it was. It reads like a Waveshare ESP32-S3-RGB-Matrix; it is a Seengreat RGB Matrix HUB75 S3, with a different pin map entirely. The giveaway is the module, N16R8 here against Waveshare's N32R16, and `esptool flash_id` will tell you which one you bought.

Then the panel came up banded red with speckled green. I took that for a colour problem and tuned white balance twice, R91 G68 B100, then R20 G38 B98, before doing it properly in linear light. None of it was the bug.

> **Trap:** red with speckled green is a power symptom, not a colour one. Drop brightness to 10%. If the colours come back, it is the supply. Ten seconds, and it saves hours.

It was browning out on a laptop USB port. Its own 5 V supply fixed the colour and the dropped bits together, and the default budget settled at 500 mA after a hub and a second laptop port both browned out at 900. Artist and title went on the top and bottom edges in a 3×5 face once the panel was honest.

entries.title: Phases 0 to 5 in one sitting
entries.body:
Phases 0 through 5, one sitting:

- **Panel:** HUB75 DMA driver, boot test pattern
- **Settings and web:** NVS storage, captive-portal WiFi manager, JSON API
- **Spotify:** a PKCE helper script, then the on-device client with refresh, polling and backoff
- **Art:** cover pulled over HTTPS into PSRAM, decoded with JPEGDEC, box-resampled to 64×64, crossfaded on track change
- **Sound:** ES7210 mics, FFT and beat detection running on the board, the effect catalog behind them

The mode state machine came last and tied the scenes together.

builds.title: vizBot
builds.summary: A companion robot with a face, personalities, and a cloud backend.
builds.body:
vizBot is a little companion robot with a face. 25 procedurally-drawn
expressions and a handful of personalities that decide how it reacts to the
room. It started as an LED matrix controller and grew a face, then a voice, then
opinions.

Everything on screen is drawn from primitives, eyes and mouths and tweened
transitions, so the same face engine renders on a Waveshare LCD, an M5 Core S3
and a 1-bit 128×64 OLED without a per-device redraw. It listens on a 512-point
FFT of the Core S3 mic, drives a StackChan servo base for head movement, and
pushes its speech to a WLED matrix over DDP, drawing the pixels itself rather
than fighting WLED's scroll effects for them.

## The fleet part

Dual-core FreeRTOS underneath: rendering on one core, WiFi and HTTP and mesh and
an isolated cloud task on the other. Two networks, doing different jobs:

- **vizCloud**, a Node.js backend I run on DigitalOcean, handles registration,
  telemetry, fleet groups and server-queued commands, including NTP-scheduled
  ones so a room of bots can move together.
- **An ESP-NOW mesh** handles the local etiquette. Flag bits in a broadcast
  packet mean two bots won't drive the same WLED matrix, and one will defer its
  speech bubble until a peer releases the display.

Four of them are living in other places now, which makes it a real fleet in the
wild rather than a demo with plans.
