entries.title: StackChan servo hardening + fleet deployment
entries.body:
Chased the StackChan head stalls to ground, and the chase was the interesting part. The head would seize after hours of running, but the servo bus still answers `ReadPos` during a stall, so my angle-floor watchdog never fired. A day of watching it proved detection was a dead end: the bus isn't deaf, the motion layer just stops producing movement. Meanwhile a manual reinit recovered it every single time, in about a second.

So it stopped trying to be clever. The rail cycles blind every 5 minutes, and the rest of the work was making that cycle not look awful:

- capture the pose *before* cutting power, then glide back to it over ~1.8 s instead of snapping home
- bow to the pitch floor first, over 1.2 s, so the head has nowhere to free-fall when torque vanishes

It reads as a slow bow now, down and back up, rather than a collapse and a recover. Also calibrated the pitch zero and moved onto the M5 StackChan-BSP driver, arming the servos properly with position mode and torque.

Four vizBots are living in other places now, with vizCloud up for pushing them content.

entries.title: vizMini — the face on an ESP32-C3 and an OLED
entries.body:
Spun off vizMini: the same face engine on an ESP32-C3 SuperMini and a 1-bit 128×64 OLED, which is about the cheapest hardware it will run on. Being drawn from primitives paid off here, since the face just renders smaller and in one colour.

The capacitive pad became a debounced pushbutton, the sleep state went away so it stays awake, and it takes OTA updates over the web.

entries.title: Neon-green build photos + cold-boot servo fix

media.caption: One of the 25 procedurally-drawn expressions

entries.body:
The bot in the flesh: neon-green shell, OLED face, StackChan base underneath.

Fixed the servos refusing to answer after a cold boot. They wake up slower than the firmware asks, so the ping retries now until they answer instead of giving up on the first miss. Also decoupled web control from cloud sync, because a slow sync was making the buttons feel dead, and fixed a registration bug that truncated device names.

entries.title: StackChan head touch: front nods, back shakes
entries.body:
The Si12T head touch was firing phantom reactions, and my zone model was wrong. The three pads run front, middle and back along the top of the head, not left to right.

- **Debounce:** M5Unified's button class instead of a hand-rolled state machine
- **Sensitivity:** raised to match the StackChan BSP reference
- **Reactions:** front tap nods, back tap shakes, each with a random phrase, a synth sound and an LED flash. Hold for 2 seconds and it goes chill.

> **Trap:** only a full-strength hit on the front or back pad counts. Anything less, and stray capacitive coupling, a ceiling fan included, fires reactions.

entries.title: Audio-reactive ambient effects + kaleidoscope pass
entries.body:
Made all 16 ambient effects audio-reactive, in three passes. The ambient set and a base-LED audio mode first, then mappings for the remaining 12, then a punch-up on Plasma, Galaxy, Stripes and Puzzle with an overlay underneath.

Added a kaleidoscope post-processing pass over the top, and a drama slider so I can dial back how much it is doing.

entries.title: vizBot 3.0 — StackChan body target
entries.body:
vizBot 3.0: the face got a body.

A StackChan base, brought up in phases. Minimum-viable build target, then driver bring-up, then web endpoints with the pitch clamped so it can't hurt itself. After that came the parts that make it feel alive: servo expressivity, touch reactions, idle sweeps, and a chill mode.

Swapped the old ambient effects for 16 patterns ported from NoodleLab.

> **Trap:** pin `M5GFX@0.2.19`. Version 0.2.21 gives the Core S3 a black screen, and nothing about the symptom points at the graphics library.

entries.title: Bodies: spaceman, crab, hologram, dinosaur, monster
entries.body:
vizBot has worn a lot of bodies. Some I use, some I put away, and some I bring back:

- the spaceman
- the crab
- the hologram
- the dinosaur
- a little monster

All of them are explorations in the same space.

entries.title: PlatformIO migration + a SAM2695 MIDI synth

media.caption: The killer feature: the bots speak on a WLED sign

entries.body:
Moved vizbot and vizpow off the Arduino IDE and onto PlatformIO, for builds I can reproduce and firmware binaries I can version. Bins publish to a top-level `builds/` directory.

Then a SAM2695 MIDI synth, over several phases, including caching and syncing MIDI sequences from the cloud. It plays tunes now as well as talking.

entries.title: LCD 1.3 target, a chill face, a louder web UI
entries.body:
Added the Waveshare ESP32-S3-LCD-1.3 as a target, using the board-first config pattern. Hologram mode flips vertically now instead of horizontally, for the Pepper's-ghost prism.

- **Chill:** replaces Sleepy, with half-lidded eyes instead of closed ones
- **Brightness:** fixed the LCD slider and raised the default to full
- **Web UI:** three tabs (Face, Settings, Network) and a neo-brutalist redesign: cream background, thick black borders, hard offset shadows

entries.title: vizCloud, multi-bot orchestration, and an ESP-NOW mesh
entries.body:
The bots learned about each other.

vizCloud integration landed first: a static BSS framebuffer so TLS doesn't flicker the screen, an isolated cloud task on core 0, one unified WiFi task. Multi-bot orchestration went on top of that.

Locally they form an ESP-NOW mesh that arbitrates for the WLED matrix, using flag bits in a broadcast packet. Two bots won't drive the same matrix, and one will hold its speech bubble until a peer lets go of the display. Watching a bot wait its turn is the first time the fleet felt like a fleet.

entries.title: Senses — mic, proximity, light, and a hologram mode
entries.body:
Gave it senses:

- **Mic:** an audio-analysis driver, with sound-reactive expressions on top
- **Proximity and light:** reactive expressions, plus auto-brightness
- **Face:** reworked to 6 eye shapes, 6 mouth shapes and 8 new expressions
- **Speech bubble:** proportional font, positioned off the sensor readings

There's a hologram mode now too, mirroring the LCD horizontally for a Pepper's-ghost prism. It is a silly trick and it looks fantastic.

entries.title: LovyanGFX migration + a tween system
entries.body:
Migrated the LCD target from Arduino_GFX to LovyanGFX, then spent the afternoon chasing a blue tint and dim brightness that came with it.

Built a tween system too, with 8 easing functions and wired it through the main loop, which retired a pile of hand-rolled smoothstep and lerp calls. Expression changes and look-around animations ride the curves now, and the difference between a linear blink and an eased one is the whole personality.

entries.title: M5 Core S3 target + per-device identity
entries.body:
Added an M5Stack Core S3 target, and with it a `layout.h` that derives the UI from the screen size. A new display is a compile flag now, not a rewrite.

Each bot also got an identity: a per-device SSID and mDNS hostname derived from the eFuse MAC, plus a name you can set yourself so it's memorable rather than hex. That's the groundwork for more than one of these existing at once.

entries.title: WLED integration — from scroll effects to raw DDP
entries.body:
Wanted the bot's speech to appear on a WLED matrix. Spent days driving WLED's built-in scrolling text effect and fighting it the whole way: scroll speed, trails, jump cuts, and the effect reinitialising between consecutive words.

Gave up on it and went to direct pixel control over DDP, drawing the text myself. Clean frames immediately.

> **Lesson:** when you're fighting somebody else's effect engine for control of individual frames, stop fighting and take the pixels.

entries.title: Networking hardening and the Core 0 crash
entries.body:
Several days of networking, and one crash that ate most of them. The web server had moved to a FreeRTOS task on core 0, and core 0 kept going down with it. I went through watchdog reconfigures and stack-size bumps before the WiFi task would stay up.

The rest of the hardening, in the order it landed:

- a sequential boot loader with onscreen diagnostics, so a failure names itself
- an I2C mutex and a command queue, so two callers can't talk over each other
- WiFi provisioning with credentials in NVS
- a captive portal with DNS and mDNS auto-redirect
- persistent settings and a health heartbeat

entries.title: Face engine and the split into vizBot
entries.body:
This is the day it stopped being a matrix controller.

Built the face engine in phases: a core face with 12 expressions, then sayings and speech bubbles, then personality presets with a web UI, then 20 expressions with backgrounds. Everything is drawn from primitives, so the face scales to whatever screen it lands on instead of being a pile of bitmaps per device.

Then split the firmware in two. vizpow keeps the effects, vizbot gets the face. The AP name changed from VizPow to vizBot, which is the moment I admitted what I was building.

entries.title: Hi-res LCD, an ESP8266 port, and the vizPow name
entries.body:
Brought up a hi-res LCD mode with a touch menu, so the effects have somewhere to live that isn't a matrix.

Then ported the engine to an ESP8266 matrix target, mostly to find out how portable it really was. It ran.

Renamed the project vizPow on the way through.

entries.title: Emoji mode, icon sprites, and shake-to-switch
entries.body:
Added an emoji mode with a sprite picker, 32 icon sprites, and tooling to manage them without hand-editing arrays.

Effects and palettes now auto-cycle out of a shuffle bag rather than a random pick, so you don't get the same one twice in a row. And the IMU got a job: shake the thing to change mode.

entries.title: Bring-up — ESP32-S3 LED matrix controller
entries.body:
Day one. An ESP32-S3, an LED matrix, and a controller that renders effects onto it. Build config sorted, folders laid out, pixels moving.

No face, no cloud, no gestures. It was a matrix controller and nothing else, which is worth remembering given where it ended up.

builds.title: ESP32 Plane Radar
builds.summary: A desktop ADS-B aircraft scope on a round LCD.
builds.body:
A desktop ADS-B scope on a round LCD. It paints live traffic around my home onto
a green sonar grid: a rotating sweep with a comet trail, heading triangles with
speed vectors out front, callsign and type and altitude tags, and anything out of
range parked as a bearing dot on the rim. Data comes from the public adsb.fi
opendata API over HTTPS, no local receiver, polled every 3 seconds for up to 64
aircraft.

The hardware is a GC9A01 1.28" round LCD (240×240, LovyanGFX) on an ESP32-C3
Super Mini, in a printed slatted case with a BOOT button and an optional touch
pad for range. An ESP32-S3 target exists too, for the better radio.

## How it's built

TLS eats RAM, so the whole thing is written around the heap:

- render into an 8-bit off-screen sprite, chosen specifically to survive the
  pressure of a live HTTPS poll
- stream-parse the JSON through a field filter, so the body is never held whole
- check the heap *before* opening the socket

Between polls each plane dead-reckons forward from its last heading and speed, so
motion stays smooth at 30 fps. That's capped: a dropped poll or an outage can't
fling a target off the edge.

There's a gzipped SPA baked into flash as well, served off the device itself:
radar, flight list, stats and detail cards off `/api/flights`, with the browser
enriching routes and photos from adsbdb and planespotters.

picturesOverTime.caption: Round GC9A01 on the bench

entries.title: Empty radar bug: de-chunk the ADS-B body
entries.body:
The radar had started coming up empty. Grid, sweep, no planes. The fetch succeeded, the heap was fine, and nothing logged an error for a full day.

The endpoint sits behind Cloudflare and had started answering with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. `getStreamPtr()` hands back the raw socket and never de-chunks, so hex chunk-size lines were landing in the middle of the JSON. With a filter in place that parses as *Ok* against an empty document, so the fetch published zero aircraft, returned true, and never backed off.

> **Trap:** a parser that succeeds on garbage is worse than one that crashes on it. The empty-`ac` case now logs instead of publishing silence.

Fixed with a small stream wrapper that de-chunks when `getSize()` reports -1 and passes identity bodies straight through, so the body still never gets held whole. `useHTTP10(true)` also kills chunking, but then the body is close-delimited and WiFiClientSecure truncates it, which trades a silent bug for a noisy one. Verified on the S3: ten clean fetches in a row, idle heap 105 KB, worst min-free 26 KB.

entries.title: Map underlay + multi-leg routes
entries.body:
Both scopes got a faint map underlay: coast, lakes, rivers, roads, dim enough to place the traffic without competing with it. A regional crop of Natural Earth 1:10m bakes into flash at about 57 KB, projects once per range change into a fixed 14 KB screen-space cache, and draws under the sweep. No heap, so the TLS headroom is untouched. Now you can see a plane following a river valley.

Building it turned up an old bug. The device projection was missing its `cos(lat)`, so everything was stretched about 26% east-west, and the device and the web app had been quietly disagreeing the whole time. Both read from one shared projection header now.

Routes learned to handle multi-leg trips too. Every stop renders, `JFK → RIC → SFO`, with the leg the aircraft is actually flying picked by smallest detour against its live position and brightened.

entries.title: The web companion app — touch radar in the browser
entries.body:
The browser side got real. There's an interactive touch radar served straight off the device now, gzipped into flash, pulling traffic from `/api/flights` and letting the browser enrich each plane with route and photo data from adsbdb and planespotters. Per-device themes, and a header with live context so you know what you're looking at. The heap fix is the part that mattered: serving the SPA and running the live ADS-B poll were fighting over the same RAM.

Then the TTP223 touch pad, which had started cycling range on its own at about two steps a second. A loose sensor makes the line oscillate, and every phantom step also wrote NVS and forced a refetch. Three defenses:

1. A press only counts after the level holds for 40 ms. Real touches last 50 ms and up; noise edges don't.
2. More than 6 taps in 8 seconds locks the input out until it's been quiet for 10. The BOOT button and the web UI stay live.
3. Range persists to NVS once, 3 seconds after it stops changing.

entries.title: Sweep goes under the grid
entries.body:
One line of layering, and it changed the whole look: the sweep renders beneath the grid now, not over it. The glow reads as light passing under the graticule, and the grid and plane markers stay crisp on top.

Draw order is half the battle with these sprite composites.

entries.title: Onboard RGB status light + a scanning overlay
entries.body:
Put the C3's onboard RGB LED to work as a status light, and laid a scanning overlay over the scope so it reads like radar instead of a plot.

Dropped the 100 km range while I was there. The projection distortion gets silly at that zoom and I never once used it. The close ranges are the useful ones.

entries.title: Forked a plane-radar project, then rebuilt it heap-first

media.caption: Round GC9A01 on the bench

entries.body:
Started from a modern-SDK fork of a plane-radar project on the ESP32-C3 and then gutted most of it. The stock build locked up every so often: it fired a burst of ADS-B requests and buffered each whole response body. One request on a backoff, plus a stream parse with a field filter so the body is never held whole, and the lockups stopped.

The rest was one long session:

- **Dual core:** the network fetch on its own task, so a poll never stalls a frame
- **Interpolation:** targets dead-reckon between the 3-second polls instead of teleporting
- **ESP32-S3 Super Mini:** a second target, for the better radio, with WiFi retry hardening
- **Looks:** 16-bit colour at 80 MHz SPI, a sweep with a comet trail, 30 fps pacing

By the end it was a live scope sitting in the printed slatted cube: round LCD, green grid, real callsigns.

builds.title: PhantasyFish
builds.body:
Fantasy sports for Phish setlists. You predict a show before the band plays, then
score on how close you got. I built and run the whole thing: the game, the
automated scoring, an AI that drafts setlists from history, the leaderboards, and
the email that ties it together. It's been live and played for over a year.

Full-stack TypeScript, React over Express and PostgreSQL with Drizzle. The
scoring engine fires automatically the moment the official setlist posts, and
hands out bonuses for:

- the right song
- the right set
- the exact position in that set
- openers and closers
- bustouts, shared with everyone who called them

**WookBot** is an OpenAI setlist generator built on historical play patterns.
Around it sit leaderboards (global, tour, show), research tools, an admin
console, and transactional email.

## Year one

| Metric | Total |
|---|---|
| Players | 115, across 6 tours and 28 venues |
| Shows scored | 74 |
| Predictions | 1,155 |
| Points earned | 65,054 |
| Top score | 248 |
| Exact positions called | 398 |
| Songs in the right set | 2,501 |
| Bustouts called | 99 |
| WookBot setlists | 67 |
| Song catalog | 959 |

entries.title: Year one, by the numbers
entries.body:
Ran the full year-one data pull. 74 shows scored, 1,155 predictions, 65,054 points.

The number I didn't expect: 398 exact song positions called correctly. Not "this song will show up", but this song, in this slot, on this night. The full tally is on the build page.

entries.title: phish.net outage resilience: local mirror, DB fallback, manual scoring
entries.body:
Hardened the game against phish.net going down mid-show, which is the worst possible failure for live scoring: the band plays on, and the game goes blind.

Three layers, in order of desperation:

1. a local phish.net mirror with background sync
2. a database fallback for show endpoints when the API is blocked
3. scoring straight from a hand-entered setlist when the network won't cooperate at all

A bad night on someone else's server doesn't take the game down with it any more.

entries.title: Import upcoming shows into a tour, modular admin routes
entries.body:
Admins can import upcoming shows straight into a tour now, so setting up a season is a few clicks instead of hand-entering a schedule.

That came after splitting the admin routes out of one enormous file into modules. The console had grown past the point where "it works" was enough.

entries.title: Tour Wrapped recap page and personalized email links
entries.body:
Built Tour Wrapped: a per-player recap of the tour just played, with your best calls, your points and your rarities. Every player gets a personalized link, keyed to the right tour, wired through the email system as a `wrappedLink` variable.

It took a few follow-up fixes to make the callout point at the correct completed tour. Worth it: Wrapped is the thing people actually shared.

entries.title: Final summer-tour data pull, season closeout
entries.body:
Ran the last data pull for summer tour and let the season settle.

The rhythm of this thing is clear now: a burst of live scoring while shows are happening, then a quiet stretch to reconcile data and fix what scored wrong. First full tour season in the books.

entries.title: Scores dashboard and a stats sidebar
entries.body:
Shipped a scores dashboard and a stats sidebar next to the research tools: a song explorer with a selector, tour-plays columns, and the numbers people use to argue about what the band will open with.

The research side is where the serious players live. They build predictions off gap data and tour history; the rest of us guess.

entries.title: Live mode: scoring as the show happens
entries.body:
Summer tour meant live mode. A live view scores predictions as the setlist comes in, with an admin side to drive it song by song, plus a compact setlist display and bustout callouts pushed right into it.

The leaderboard reshuffles while the band is still playing. That is the best the game has ever felt.

entries.title: Tour manager and per-tour song counts
entries.body:
Built a tour manager, and started tracking per-tour song counts.

Phish is organized by tour, so almost everything worth showing depends on knowing which shows belong to which run: leaderboards, research tools, Wrapped. This is unglamorous structural work that half the later features quietly stand on.

entries.title: Email manager 1.0
entries.body:
Stood up transactional email properly on Resend: a composer, refined templates, and a log viewer so I can see what actually went out. The old ad-hoc emailers are gone.

Added a rate limiter the next day, before a big send got the domain flagged.

entries.title: Editing setlists by hand
entries.body:
Added an admin interface for editing setlist details by hand, because the official data is sometimes wrong and sometimes just late, and every scoring run depends on it.

A mangled setlist can be corrected, or a generated one refined, before it scores. Malformed source data fails with an error I can read instead of a stack trace.

entries.title: Admin console 1.0
entries.body:
Built the back office: admin screens for files, songs, users and WookBot setlists in one place.

Running a live game means touching data constantly, fixing a song entry, checking an account, curating a generated setlist, and I was doing all of it with one-off scripts against the database. This replaced them with actual screens.

entries.title: Scoring engine: bustout detection from gap data, bonus breakdown
entries.body:
Reworked the scoring engine to be fairer about rarity. Bustout detection runs off gap data now, the stretch of shows since a song was last played, so calling a genuine rarity is worth real points. Shared bustouts pay everyone who called it, rather than rewarding whoever saved first.

Tightened exact-position accuracy at the same time, and started showing the bonus breakdown on the score page. If a player can't see why they got the points, the total may as well be random.

entries.title: WookBot: OpenAI setlist generator goes public
entries.body:
WookBot went public: an OpenAI-backed generator that drafts a plausible setlist for an upcoming show out of historical play patterns. It gets a home-page module with the show date and venue, a selector for browsing past generations, and skeleton states while it thinks.

It only pulls from published show data, so it suggests songs the band actually plays instead of inventing a dream set.

entries.title: Leaderboards: global, tour, single-show
entries.body:
Leaderboards, in three scopes: global, current tour, and single show. Each ranks the top predictors for its scope, and every name links straight to that player's scorecard.

One click from a rank to the actual prediction is the whole point. Otherwise a leaderboard is just a list of strangers with numbers.

entries.title: Random-fill button, setlist-save fixes, spam-folder reminder
entries.body:
Closing out the first playable week, mostly on other people's behalf:

- a random-fill button, for anyone who wants to play without building a setlist by hand
- a pile of setlist-saving bugs that had been silently dropping songs
- a check-your-spam-folder note on the verification email

That last one wasn't a guess. Sign-ups were arriving and the verification mail was going straight to spam.

entries.title: Scorecards and the first scored show
entries.body:
Built the scorecard: set 1 and set 2 side by side, with a breakdown of which songs earned what. Fed it real 2024 show data so a finished prediction could actually be scored against something.

The score button stays hidden until a show is officially scored. Nobody needs to look at a wall of zeros for a show the band hasn't played yet.

entries.title: First commit: build-a-setlist UI, song database, prediction saving
entries.body:
First commit, and the core loop worked the same day: build a setlist, save it as a prediction.

The build-a-setlist UI went up first. Drop songs into slots, reorder them, add sets as you go. Then the song database, seeded out of several phish.net endpoints and cached to a local JSON file so the game isn't hammering their API on every page load.

builds.title: StackLED
builds.summary: A handheld LED stacker arcade game.
builds.body:
It's the carnival Stacker, the skill-tester where you pile a sliding light bar up
a tower. A lit bar slides left and right across a tall 8×32 field, you mash the
button to drop it, and only the pixels that overlap the row below survive.
Overhang gets trimmed, so the bar gets narrower every time you're sloppy. Reach
the top to clear the level. Five hand-authored levels, each faster and thinner
than the last, then it goes procedurally endless.

An ESP32-C3 Super Mini drives four MAX7219 panels, with an illuminated button and
a speaker that can scream.

## The bar is the health meter

The twist I'm proudest of. There's no separate lives counter: the same bar you're
stacking erodes on wall-bounces and misses, and when its width hits zero you're
done.

Under it all is bitmask math, no pixel arrays at all. Each row is a `uint8_t`:

- a new row AND'd with the one below leaves the survivors
- popcount gives the width
- count-trailing-zeros gives the left edge

I built it at makedown, a crew maker-weekend where everyone hauls in their own
project. I brought a bag of panels and a green 3D-printed wand, and left with a
game.

picturesOverTime.caption: Mid-game on the 8×32

entries.title: Shipped — battery-powered wand, repo cleanup

media.caption: Mid-game on the 8×32

entries.body: Called it done. It runs off a battery inside the green printed wand now, no laptop tether, and the repo stopped tracking `.DS_Store` on the way out.

entries.title: Attract mode and auto-detecting NO/NC button wiring
entries.body:
Added an attract mode: on power-up it plays a self-animating tower demo behind the start screen, replays after two title scrolls, and the game-over screen falls back to it after two passes. It never sits on a dead screen.

The button wiring auto-detects now. At boot the firmware reads the button and treats whatever it sees as "not pressed", so it works with a normally-open or normally-closed switch and I don't have to remember which one I soldered into which wand.

entries.title: Replaced lives with an eroding health bar
entries.body:
Killed the lives counter. The bar is the health bar now: wall-bounces and misses eat its width directly, and at width zero you're done. One number on screen instead of two, and it's the number you're already watching. The life pips moved to a 2 px strip above the current row, where a tall stack can't bury them.

Then the difficulty ramp, which I authored twice. Thick pieces are easy pieces, and my first cut got mean too fast:

| Level | First cut | Softened |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3-row blocks | 4-row blocks |
| 2 | 2-row | 3-row |
| 3 | single rows | 2-row |
| 4 | single rows | single rows |

entries.title: Full 8×32 bring-up — lives, intensity, grace rows
entries.body:
Full bring-up on the 8×32. Flipped both display axes so the tower grows upward, fixed the NC button contact, ran a siren test on the speaker. Then tuning, all of it from watching people play:

- **Lives:** four complete misses a game, with a pip flashed on each one
- **Intensity:** 6 to 10, because at 6 it washes out in a lit room
- **Grace rows:** the first three rows are free, so a fresh player can't lose on the first move
- **Stale presses:** swallowed across state transitions. A leftover press on the game-over screen was skipping the next screen entirely.

entries.title: Swapped to an FC16 4-in-1 — 8×32 playfield
entries.body:
Swapped in an FC16 4-in-1 module and reconfigured for the real playfield: four MAX7219 8×8 matrices chained into a field 8 wide and 32 tall.

Wiring a fresh chain is fiddly, so the bring-up kept a checkerboard retry loop while I was hot-plugging the matrix on the bench, then went back to the standard loop once the solder held. The button LED moved off GPIO10 to GPIO1, and the pin tables and wiring diagram now match what's actually soldered.

entries.title: Milestone 1 — full game firmware in one session
entries.body:
Scaffold to finished game firmware in one session: engine, level progression, scoring.

The whole field is bits. Each row is a `uint8_t`, and landing a piece is three operations:

- AND the candidate row with the row below, and what survives is the overlap
- popcount that, and you have the new width
- count trailing zeros, and you have the left edge

No pixel arrays anywhere, just bit twiddling on a non-blocking `millis()` state machine. High score goes to NVS so it survives a power cycle.

Wrote the build guide out in full while the wiring was fresh, down to drawing the resistor bodies with correct 5-band colour codes so the BOM reads straight off the page. Renamed the whole thing STACKLED somewhere in there.

builds.title: The Cyberdeck (noode-exp)
builds.summary: A portable Raspberry Pi workstation with a custom ESP32 electronics bench.
builds.body:
A portable computer I built to be my bench, not just to sit on it.

The deck half is an assembly job, no code of mine in it:

- **Raspberry Pi 5**, 8 GB, with a 7" touchscreen
- **Mii Bluetooth keyboard** in a printed tray
- **M5Stack Stick / Joy-C** as the mouse

The repo name, `noodle-exp`, belongs to the other half. **noode-exp** is a
standalone ESP32-S3 gadget that lives on the deck as its electronics workbench: a
Lonely Binary ESP32-S3 N16R8 driving a 2" ST7789, an EC11 encoder and a KY-023
joystick, a 4×4 WS2812 matrix, a pair of LED filament "noodles" (hence the name),
and an HLK-LD2412 mmWave presence radar.

It runs 11 modes off about 2500 lines of monolithic C++, dual-core with a PSRAM
framebuffer:

| Kind | Modes |
|---|---|
| **3D** | Steer Cube, Cube Swarm, Warp Tunnel, Box Physics |
| **Pattern** | Chladni, Kaleido |
| **Light** | Filaments, LED Matrix, Color Pick |
| **Sensor** | Room Radar, Presence Log |

No WiFi, no Bluetooth, no companion app. It is a genuinely standalone appliance,
which is rarer than it should be.

The v1 case geometry came out broken. v2 got a redesigned keyboard tray, and that
one is the hero.

picturesOverTime.caption: v1: the Pi tablet and the noode-exp bench
Chladni, one of 42 standing-wave figures

entries.title: mmWave presence work feeds a planned vizBot add-on
entries.body:
Room Radar and Presence Log exist to prove out the HLK-LD2412 mmWave sensor. Both modes just show what the sensor sees: presence in the room, and a rolling log of when it changed.

> **Next:** spin the presence detection out into a vizBot add-on, so the robot knows when someone is nearby. noode-exp is the bench where that gets proven first.

entries.title: v2 case with the redesigned keyboard tray
entries.body:
Redrew the broken v1 geometry into a v2 case with a proper keyboard tray, and it sits and folds the way it was supposed to. The Mii keyboard drops into the tray, the 7" screen mounts above it, the bench box docks alongside.

This is the configuration I actually carry.

entries.title: noode-exp bench running — 11 modes and a Chladni pattern

media.caption: Chladni, one of 42 standing-wave figures

entries.body:
The bench is alive. All 11 modes cycle off the encoder, Steer Cube through Room Radar, with the LEDs running on core 0 and the ST7789 pushed to 80 MHz SPI so nothing tears while a mode is animating.

The matrix effects are ported from NoodleLab.

No WiFi, no Bluetooth, no app. It boots into its own modes and that's the whole contract.

entries.title: Case color scheme — black with neon-yellow, skull on the bench box
entries.body:
Set the colour scheme across both enclosures: black with neon-yellow accents, and a skull on the electronics box to match the branding on everything else I build.

Stood the folded case next to the bench box, and for the first time the two read as one rig instead of two projects.

entries.title: v1 rig assembled — Pi tablet plus the ESP32 bench

media.caption: v1: the Pi tablet and the noode-exp bench

entries.body:
Got the v1 rig standing: the Pi tablet beside the noode-exp bench, a case each.

The case geometry is wrong. Parts don't seat cleanly and it won't fold flat, which was the entire point of the hinge. Logging it here rather than fixing it in place, because the tray needs redrawing from scratch.

entries.title: First Pi 5 build — 7" touch, Bluetooth keyboard, Joy-C mouse
entries.body:
Started assembling the deck around an 8 GB Raspberry Pi 5, with a 7" touchscreen as the only display. Text comes from a Mii Bluetooth keyboard, pointing from an M5Stack Stick running a Joy-C, which is a stand-in mouse and a strange little one.

That's the whole input story. No external host, no Pi software yet: this half of the rig is hardware assembly.

recent.title: Last desktop case: the hinge holds the screen up

media.caption: The mobile version

recent.body:
Called the desktop case done. This is the last version of it.

Extended the base of the hinge, so an open lid has something behind it to lean on instead of flopping back. It looks better with that mass there too. Then the detailing: a silver skull inlay on the lid and a silver strip running along the base.

> **Next:** a mobile version with a battery, built on this one.

recent.title: Six wall patterns + a list browser on the dial

media.caption: The list, and the view after a tap launches it

recent.body:
Pulled six more patterns off the Patternflow wall: Fractal Storm, Branched Flow, Hypno Circles, Tri March, Vector Field Flow and Pattern 0522. Hypno Circles only exists as JavaScript, so that one is a hand port.

The importer had been seeing 44 of the wall's 194 patterns. The site caps a page at 44 whatever you ask for, and the loop read a short page as the end.

The bank is at 51 slots and still growing, which a grid on a round screen can't hold. The dial got a BANK mode instead: the knob scrolls a list, a tap launches, and once something is playing the knob does nothing. That also killed the old bug where a fast spin skipped patterns. Flashed the dial, Console and hub75, and the panel still lights with 14 KB more static RAM.

> **Next:** the rotation playlist is a 64-bit mask, so 64 slots is the ceiling until the protocol changes.

recent.title: Twisted Tunnel: a Bauhaus zoom, rebuilt

media.caption: Tilt 0, 0.25 and 0.5, then Color at 0.2 and 0.8

recent.body:
Started from a canvas sketch of Bauhaus rectangles zooming inward and ported it to the Patternflow bank as Nested Frames, bank 44. Named it Twisted Tunnel for the Patternflow wall.

The sketch claimed to loop seamlessly and didn't. Every five seconds each ring took on its neighbour's colour and shape. Keying every ring on its own index fixed it.

Then it drifted a long way from the original:

- **Tilt:** a twist keyed on ring size, so the frames form a spiral that turns as it falls.
- **Colour:** the red, blue and yellow from the Mondrian pattern, with true black and white.
- **Randomness:** each ring gets its own spacing, lean, shape and slow drift.
- **Fills:** about one ring in five carries dots, a grid, stripes or a checker.

I dropped the yellow square the sketch kept fixed at the centre. It looked weird sitting still while everything else moved.

> **Trap:** one float for zoom depth loses most of each frame's step near its wrap at the lowest speed, and the zoom stutters. Split it into a whole part and a fraction.

recent.title: Clamshell together, and a README

media.caption: 44 icons cached, last synced 52 seconds ago

recent.body:
Got the clamshell together. A printed threaded rod runs through a two-part hinge with a knurled head on one end, and there are detents at the knuckle interface so tightening actually holds the angle. Plain chamfers top and bottom, because the curved edges never printed clean and I stopped pretending they would.

Backed out the touch changes I made for the second board. The first board didn't want them.

Then the README, origin story included: a pocket sketchbook where the page is 8×8 and the ink is light.

recent.title: README catches up with Noodle 2K
recent.body:
The README still described NoodleLab: filaments, the ToF sensor, the icon and 12×8 sats, 16 effects, a hardcoded channel. All of that has been gone since the August rebuild, and CLAUDE.md was the only honest document in the repo.

Rewrote it around what's actually on the tray, with the three-name arc up front so the old photos and posts still make sense. Merged the Mondrian branch to main on the way past, and deleted four merged branches that had been sitting there since spring.

recent.title: Projective touch calibration, and LED rotation per device
recent.body:
Touch was the day. Moved to pressure-based reads, threw out the four-corner min and max map for a projective calibration, and made the handheld run calibration on first boot instead of shipping my bring-up constants to every board.

LED rotation became a per-device setting in NVS too, because every matrix ends up mounted a different way in a different case, and a constant only ever describes the one on my desk.

recent.title: Another round of case bodies
recent.body:
Printed another round of case bodies and lined them up against the last one. No electronics in any of them. These were only to see how the shells come off the plate and how the lid sits shut.

Printing a clamshell is mostly a hinge problem. Everything else is a box.

recent.title: Mondrian, take two

media.caption: One layout at five settings of the Color knob

recent.body:
Reworked the motion. The old version slid one section out and back like a tray, and sometimes nothing actually changed on screen. Now every line moves at once while part of the grid rebuilds and a colour block slides to a new cell.

That turned up a bug where remixing the whole canvas skipped moving the lines at all.

The Color knob is one smooth sweep now, built on the spacing between Mondrian's own red, blue and yellow, with his palette sitting in the middle of the range.

Flashed it to the rig and every colour was wrong. Took me a minute to notice the global palette tint was still switched on, quietly re-mapping a pattern that brings its own colours.

recent.title: A day of just using it
recent.body:
No commits. A day of just using it.

Thirty-nine icons synced, stepping through them with the transitions running and the sync age up in the title bar. The matrix is still living in its own frame on printed knurled thumb screws.

The firmware is doing what it should. The enclosure is the open question.

recent.title: A Mondrian pattern for the Patternflow bank

media.caption: Three compositions from one run

recent.body:
Wrote my first pattern from scratch for the Patternflow bank: a Mondrian grid that keeps rearranging itself.

It builds a layout by splitting the canvas in two, then splitting the pieces, which is roughly how the paintings are put together. Whatever it lands on is a valid composition rather than a scatter of rectangles.

Worked it out in JavaScript first, in a small browser harness, then hand-ported it to C++ for the hub75. The two versions match pixel for pixel, which is the only reason I trust the port.

recent.title: m5bigfun on CoreS3, and a chooser
recent.body:
Ported the console to m5bigfun: a CoreS3 sitting in a Faces Bottom3 with a Gamepad3, and two rows of five SK6812 to play with.

The LEDs got a job rather than a glow. Effects are ranked by tier, every game has a voice on the strips, and Backgammon uses them to show whose turn it is.

Since the device also holds the vizBot firmware, there's a top-level chooser in the factory partition now: one board, two firmwares, pick at boot.

recent.title: Renamed to 8x8 labz, and color families

media.caption: First build

recent.body:
Renamed 8x8 Studio to 8x8 labz, and redid both front ends neobrutalist: cream paper, black ink, thick borders, hard offset shadows, Slackey headings, lowercase everywhere, and a matching boot title card on the handheld.

The palette got split into families of six OKLCH shades. Picking a colour on a 320×240 resistive panel is now a family dropdown and twelve swatches, instead of hunting a 256-colour grid with a fingernail.

Home is four big tiles with a live mirror of the LEDs.

recent.title: Phases 5 and 6 — matrix player, touch editor, edit uploads

media.caption: 32 icons over two pages

recent.body:
Phases 5 and 6, one sitting. The matrix got a player with nine transitions and sixteen ambient patterns ported from vizpow.

Then the screens went in around it: browse, detail, settings and touch calibration. The editor came last, with pencil, fill, picker, eraser, undo and animation frames.

Two bugs worth keeping:

- the LVGL draw buffer has to be aligned, or the screen comes up blank and noisy with no error anywhere
- screens must be freed on leave, because the sync task needs about fifty kilobytes free for its TLS handshake and a leftover screen is exactly what it doesn't have

recent.title: Icon format, web app, and first light on the CYD
recent.body:
Whole spine in a day, both ends of it.

The web side first: the icon format and its shared library, a C header export, and a Postgres-backed API under the catalog, editor and palette pages. Deployed onto DigitalOcean App Platform the same afternoon.

Then the firmware. Scaffold, CYD bring-up, WiFi setup, and a first sync landing real icons in a LittleFS cache.

The panel fought back for an hour. Colours only come out right as BGR with inversion on, and the ILI9341 has no reset pin, so it keeps whatever inversion state it had across a warm reset and has to be told again at every boot.

recent.title: Phone pairing by QR — and the panel in a finished case

media.caption: De La Soul, The Magic Number

recent.body:
A board you hand to someone shouldn't need a computer. So the panel shows a QR code, alternating with a typable base32 card for anyone who would rather not scan:

1. The phone scans it and signs into Spotify on kpow.xyz
2. The credentials come back as an AES-256-GCM envelope the relay can't read
3. The board decrypts, applies, verifies against Spotify, and acks

The first real phone test died on that last step: `ack ok -> http -1`, with the phone sitting on "Board is connecting". The Spotify client was holding the only TLS context again. Now the ack frees the keep-alive before it posts and retries for about 15 seconds. Re-tested on the second board: Welcome back, then You're connected.

The case is finished too. Printed frame and stand, skulls cut into the side panel, and a choice of silver, white, grey or translucent diffusers.

recent.title: Search straight from the browser, per-card saves, and the docs
recent.body:
Put Spotify search on the control page, with the browser calling Spotify directly through a token endpoint so the board carries none of it.

Most of the work was in what Spotify does when you ask it to play something:

- a limit above 10 comes back 400, so the search asks for 10
- playback needs an explicit device id, and a stale one has to be retried
- a browser player accepts a queue and then refuses to play, so the picker prefers real Spotify apps and warns you when you've chosen one

The page got per-card Save buttons and speed sliders for the visualizer and ambient while I was in there. Then the docs, all four: README, user guide, hardware guide, web API reference.

recent.title: Memory cards in ambient, kaleidoscope, and a neo-brutalist control page
recent.body:
Ambient got a memory. It keeps 20 tracks with their covers, seeded from Spotify's recently-played at boot, and fades one back in with how long ago you played it. NTP for the clock, PSRAM for the API bodies.

The rest of the day:

- **Kaleidoscope:** a post-filter over any effect, NoodleLab's fold modes, live controls on the page
- **Puzzle:** 16 px tiles on the 64×64, proportional borders, faster eased slides
- **Snakes:** rendered at 32×32 and upscaled, so the bodies are 2 px and you can see them
- **Control page:** neo-brutalist restyle, collapsible cards, transport buttons

Then a stuck-on-song bug. After a token expired the display never moved on, because the refresh was going out while the API session was still open.

> **Lesson:** there is room for exactly one TLS context. The API, the token endpoint and the art CDN take turns, and whoever wants it drops the other's keep-alive first.

recent.title: Status screens, random palettes, and a wheel that stopped missing presses
recent.body:
The thumb wheel kept missing presses and the decoder was not the problem. `loop()` was starved under the visualizer and the FFT, so the poll just wasn't running often enough. Moved it to its own 10 ms key task with latched presses, a rock guard, and a veto so a push doesn't read as a rock.

Three smaller things around it:

- **Status screens:** boot splash, WiFi connecting, setup, unreachable, and the three Spotify states, all redrawn
- **Palettes:** a new random one on every effect change, held per side through the crossfade
- **Brightness:** default up to 100%, ambient uncapped

recent.title: Landscape TFT + chrome refresh; the Patternflow bank

media.caption: Kaleidoscope on the 64×32 hub75 and the 16×16, the dial mirroring
Second hub75 board up, both panels running

recent.body:
Recomposed the whole UI for a landscape 320×240 mount, because the ribbon was blocking the view in portrait: one-row header, framed menus, Live Control and Chladni both re-laid out. Landscape puts text beside its neighbours instead of into dead space, so every variable-length name now goes through a fitter before it's drawn.

The Patternflow bank landed the same week: JS shader-style patterns hand-ported to C++, running on all three boards. The red Qwiic button got demoted from "previous pattern" to a palette dice, because I never once used it as a back button. The dial already has back.

recent.title: First light: not the board the listing said, and USB can't feed it

media.caption: First light
Browning out on a laptop USB port

recent.body:
The board is not what the listing said it was. It reads like a Waveshare ESP32-S3-RGB-Matrix; it is a Seengreat RGB Matrix HUB75 S3, with a different pin map entirely. The giveaway is the module, N16R8 here against Waveshare's N32R16, and `esptool flash_id` will tell you which one you bought.

Then the panel came up banded red with speckled green. I took that for a colour problem and tuned white balance twice, R91 G68 B100, then R20 G38 B98, before doing it properly in linear light. None of it was the bug.

> **Trap:** red with speckled green is a power symptom, not a colour one. Drop brightness to 10%. If the colours come back, it is the supply. Ten seconds, and it saves hours.

It was browning out on a laptop USB port. Its own 5 V supply fixed the colour and the dropped bits together, and the default budget settled at 500 mA after a hub and a second laptop port both browned out at 900. Artist and title went on the top and bottom edges in a 3×5 face once the panel was honest.

recent.title: Phases 0 to 5 in one sitting
recent.body:
Phases 0 through 5, one sitting:

- **Panel:** HUB75 DMA driver, boot test pattern
- **Settings and web:** NVS storage, captive-portal WiFi manager, JSON API
- **Spotify:** a PKCE helper script, then the on-device client with refresh, polling and backoff
- **Art:** cover pulled over HTTPS into PSRAM, decoded with JPEGDEC, box-resampled to 64×64, crossfaded on track change
- **Sound:** ES7210 mics, FFT and beat detection running on the board, the effect catalog behind them

The mode state machine came last and tied the scenes together.

recent.title: Third-batch board enrolled
recent.body:
Enrolled a third-batch tinyfun board as panel profile B.

Every batch of panels drifts a little in colour and gamma. Cutting a new profile beats re-fighting the same tuning on each board.

recent.title: StackChan servo hardening + fleet deployment
recent.body:
Chased the StackChan head stalls to ground, and the chase was the interesting part. The head would seize after hours of running, but the servo bus still answers `ReadPos` during a stall, so my angle-floor watchdog never fired. A day of watching it proved detection was a dead end: the bus isn't deaf, the motion layer just stops producing movement. Meanwhile a manual reinit recovered it every single time, in about a second.

So it stopped trying to be clever. The rail cycles blind every 5 minutes, and the rest of the work was making that cycle not look awful:

- capture the pose *before* cutting power, then glide back to it over ~1.8 s instead of snapping home
- bow to the pitch floor first, over 1.2 s, so the head has nowhere to free-fall when torque vanishes

It reads as a slow bow now, down and back up, rather than a collapse and a recover. Also calibrated the pitch zero and moved onto the M5 StackChan-BSP driver, arming the servos properly with position mode and torque.

Four vizBots are living in other places now, with vizCloud up for pushing them content.

recent.title: 21 effects, a palette system, and 'Noodle 2K'
recent.body:
A content wave, and a name.

The effect catalog went to 21 with a trimmed 2D particle engine and the WLED particle effects on top of it, plus a real 16-band GEQ analyzer. Then the palette system: one global palette every effect renders through, with host-parity tests proving palette 0 reproduces the old look exactly, and a picker on the dial.

Rebranded the rig Noodle 2K, with a new layered power-on intro to match. Also brought up a hub75 MatrixPortal satellite doing native 64×32, which is four times the pixels of anything else on the tray.

recent.title: Empty radar bug: de-chunk the ADS-B body
recent.body:
The radar had started coming up empty. Grid, sweep, no planes. The fetch succeeded, the heap was fine, and nothing logged an error for a full day.

The endpoint sits behind Cloudflare and had started answering with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. `getStreamPtr()` hands back the raw socket and never de-chunks, so hex chunk-size lines were landing in the middle of the JSON. With a filter in place that parses as *Ok* against an empty document, so the fetch published zero aircraft, returned true, and never backed off.

> **Trap:** a parser that succeeds on garbage is worse than one that crashes on it. The empty-`ac` case now logs instead of publishing silence.

Fixed with a small stream wrapper that de-chunks when `getSize()` reports -1 and passes identity bodies straight through, so the body still never gets held whole. `useHTTP10(true)` also kills chunking, but then the body is close-delimited and WiFiClientSecure truncates it, which trades a silent bug for a noisy one. Verified on the S3: ten clean fetches in a row, idle heap 105 KB, worst min-free 26 KB.

recent.title: Shake to restart, and a printable case
recent.body:
A QMI8658C shake HAL: physically shaking the console restarts the current game. bigfun has no IMU, so it gets a no-op stub and the games don't care which one they're on.

The engine resumes from NVS too, so a game picks up where you left it. And the enclosure is packaged as a sliceable 3MF project now, one print from a shell.

recent.title: Killed a FeatherS3 with 48 pixels
recent.body:
Killed a FeatherS3. The 12×4's 5 V and ground were on the Feather's own pins, and 48 WS2812s at full brightness ask about 2.9 A from a rail good for roughly one. It browned out under bright frames for a while, then died, and wouldn't enumerate again even in ROM bootloader mode.

The wing is physically stuck on the Feather's rail, so that one is capped in software instead. Everything else draws from the PSU.

> **Trap:** `FastLED.setMaxPowerInVoltsAndMilliamps()` will not save you here. It applies one global budget and has no idea two strips sit on different supplies, so it looks like protection and isn't.

recent.title: The big rebuild — bare MCU, Chladni, cyberpunk chrome
recent.body:
Stripped the rig to a bare MCU and brought it back subsystem by subsystem. Things that did not come back: the icon sat, and later the 8×12, with the 16×16 moving onto a console pin instead.

What changed on the way:

- **SparkFun inputs** onto their own I2C bus, because the CAP1203 was picking up EMI from the Adafruit bus and reporting touches nobody made
- **Screensaver** replaced with a live Chladni resonant-plate visualiser
- **UI** redone on an anti-aliased chrome kit, which finally killed the flicker

A rebuild is the only time you get to un-choose things. I took it.

recent.title: megafun folds in, three boards
recent.body:
Folded megafun into the monorepo. All three boards share one core now, and the differences live in capability flags each board declares rather than in forks of the code.

Per-board panel profiles landed with it, plus an on-board tuner, and the original tinyfun board is enrolled as profile M1. The launcher auto-rotates its attract cards after idle. recent.title: megafun: a tilted screen and a joystick
recent.body:

I wanted a marbles game, and you can't do marbles without a joystick. It led to exploring a lot of other things on the same base:

- **Marbles:** the tilt maze that started it
- **Chladni:** a resonant-plate pattern generator
- **LED Studio:** a menu for driving the LED cap on top

recent.title: Backgammon VS PLAYER over ESP-NOW
recent.body:
Backgammon plays over an ESP-NOW link now. Built phase by phase: turn transport first, then game-over sync, then the doubling cube, mirroring the megafun implementation so the two stay at parity.

Then a per-device mirror and a resilience layer, so one dropped packet doesn't leave two boards disagreeing about where the checkers are.

recent.title: Map underlay + multi-leg routes
recent.body:
Both scopes got a faint map underlay: coast, lakes, rivers, roads, dim enough to place the traffic without competing with it. A regional crop of Natural Earth 1:10m bakes into flash at about 57 KB, projects once per range change into a fixed 14 KB screen-space cache, and draws under the sweep. No heap, so the TLS headroom is untouched. Now you can see a plane following a river valley.

Building it turned up an old bug. The device projection was missing its `cos(lat)`, so everything was stretched about 26% east-west, and the device and the web app had been quietly disagreeing the whole time. Both read from one shared projection header now.

Routes learned to handle multi-leg trips too. Every stop renders, `JFK → RIC → SFO`, with the leg the aircraft is actually flying picked by smallest detour against its live position and brightened.

recent.title: The web companion app — touch radar in the browser
recent.body:
The browser side got real. There's an interactive touch radar served straight off the device now, gzipped into flash, pulling traffic from `/api/flights` and letting the browser enrich each plane with route and photo data from adsbdb and planespotters. Per-device themes, and a header with live context so you know what you're looking at. The heap fix is the part that mattered: serving the SPA and running the live ADS-B poll were fighting over the same RAM.

Then the TTP223 touch pad, which had started cycling range on its own at about two steps a second. A loose sensor makes the line oscillate, and every phantom step also wrote NVS and forced a refetch. Three defenses:

1. A press only counts after the level holds for 40 ms. Real touches last 50 ms and up; noise edges don't.
2. More than 6 taps in 8 seconds locks the input out until it's been quiet for 10. The BOOT button and the web UI stay live.
3. Range persists to NVS once, 3 seconds after it stops changing.

recent.title: phish.net outage resilience: local mirror, DB fallback, manual scoring
recent.body:
Hardened the game against phish.net going down mid-show, which is the worst possible failure for live scoring: the band plays on, and the game goes blind.

Three layers, in order of desperation:

1. a local phish.net mirror with background sync
2. a database fallback for show endpoints when the API is blocked
3. scoring straight from a hand-entered setlist when the network won't cooperate at all

A bad night on someone else's server doesn't take the game down with it any more.

recent.title: Attract mode and auto-detecting NO/NC button wiring

Added an attract mode: on power-up it plays a self-animating tower demo behind the start screen, replays after two title scrolls, and the game-over screen falls back to it after two passes. It never sits on a dead screen.

The button wiring auto-detects now. At boot the firmware reads the button and treats whatever it sees as "not pressed", so it works with a normally-open or normally-closed switch and I don't have to remember which one I soldered into which wand.

Killed the lives counter. The bar is the health bar now: wall-bounces and misses eat its width directly, and at width zero you're done. recent.title: Full 8×32 bring-up — lives, intensity, grace rows

Full bring-up on the 8×32. Flipped both display axes so the tower grows upward, fixed the NC button contact, ran a siren test on the speaker. Then tuning, all of it from watching people play:

- **Lives:** four complete misses a game, with a pip flashed on each one

recent.title: mmWave presence work feeds a planned vizBot add-on
recent.body:
Room Radar and Presence Log exist to prove out the HLK-LD2412 mmWave sensor. Both modes just show what the sensor sees: presence in the room, and a rolling log of when it changed.

> **Next:** spin the presence detection out into a vizBot add-on, so the robot knows when someone is nearby. noode-exp is the bench where that gets proven first.

recent.title: Swapped to an FC16 4-in-1 — 8×32 playfield
recent.body:
Swapped in an FC16 4-in-1 module and reconfigured for the real playfield: four MAX7219 8×8 matrices chained into a field 8 wide and 32 tall.

Wiring a fresh chain is fiddly, so the bring-up kept a checkerboard retry loop while I was hot-plugging the matrix on the bench, then went back to the standard loop once the solder held. The button LED moved off GPIO10 to GPIO1, and the pin tables and wiring diagram now match what's actually soldered.

recent.title: Milestone 1 — full game firmware in one session
recent.body:
Scaffold to finished game firmware in one session: engine, level progression, scoring.

The whole field is bits. Each row is a `uint8_t`, and landing a piece is three operations:

- AND the candidate row with the row below, and what survives is the overlap
- popcount that, and you have the new width
- count trailing zeros, and you have the left edge

No pixel arrays anywhere, just bit twiddling on a non-blocking `millis()` state machine. High score goes to NVS so it survives a power cycle.

Wrote the build guide out in full while the wiring was fresh, down to drawing the resistor bodies with correct 5-band colour codes so the BOM reads straight off the page. Renamed the whole thing STACKLED somewhere in there.

recent.title: vizMini — the face on an ESP32-C3 and an OLED
recent.body:
Spun off vizMini: the same face engine on an ESP32-C3 SuperMini and a 1-bit 128×64 OLED, which is about the cheapest hardware it will run on. Being drawn from primitives paid off here, since the face just renders smaller and in one colour.
